case_studies.title: Phoenix: Safe GitHub Issue Resolution via Multi-Agent LLMs
case_studies.abstract: We present Phoenix, a multi-agent LLM system that resolves GitHub issues from triage through pull-request creation, combining seven layered safety controls with a baseline-aware test evaluation strategy. Phoenix decomposes the work across six specialized agents. Planner, reproducer, coder, tester, failure analyst and Pull Request (PR) agent, all coordinated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Every change is checked against a baseline test run before a pull request is opened. On a 24-instance slice of SWE-bench Lite. run on the production webhook path, Phoenix oracle-resolves 75% of
case_studies.summary: Phoenix is a system that solves the problem of resolving GitHub issues by automating the process from triage to pull-request creation using multi-agent language models, it was built using six specialized agents and seven safety controls, and the result was that it successfully resolved 75% of issues on a test dataset. The system aims to improve the efficiency and safety of GitHub issue resolution. It uses a baseline-aware test evaluation strategy to ensure changes do not introduce new issues.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage GitHub repositories, here is what to do: review the Phoenix system to see if it can be integrated into your workflow, assess the potential benefits of automating issue resolution, and evaluate the safety controls to ensure they meet your organization's standards. This flags a risk: if your organization relies heavily on manual GitHub issue resolution, check your current processes for potential bottlenecks and inefficiencies. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work outside of GitHub repository management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel use of multi-agent LLMs in GitHub issue resolution, direct relevance to IT engineers, valuable insights for automating issue resolution and improving safety controls. Could easily be applicable within 90 days for IT teams managing SaaS platforms like GitHub.

case_studies.title: LLM agent safety, multi-turn red-teaming, jailbreak benchmarks, adversarial robustness, safety-critical systems
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed as supervisory components for safety-critical systems, yet their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure remains poorly characterized. We present NRT-Bench, a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents acting as operators of a safety-critical system, instantiated in a simulated nuclear power plant control room. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language model agent safety in safety-critical systems by building a benchmark called NRT-Bench to test their robustness under adversarial pressure. The result is a better understanding of LLM agent vulnerabilities in simulated high-stakes environments like nuclear power plant control rooms. This research may have implications for IT infrastructure work in safety-critical systems, but it is not directly applicable to general cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for safety-critical systems, such as those used in nuclear power plants, this research flags a risk: if your org uses large language model agents, check their adversarial robustness immediately to ensure system safety. Check if your LLM agents are vulnerable to multi-turn red-teaming attacks and consider using benchmarks like NRT-Bench to test their safety. This may require collaborating with the development team to implement additional security measures.

case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of providing effective guidance to coding agents, by introducing a 'probe-and-refine' method to improve the accuracy of repository guidance, resulting in better performance of coding agents. The researchers built a system to test and refine the guidance provided to coding agents. case_studies.title: Sovereign Execution Brokers: Enforcing Certificate-Bound Authority in Agentic Control Planes
case_studies.abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly connected to cloud, deployment, and data-control workflows, but production mutation authority should not reside inside non-deterministic reasoning processes. Existing access-control mechanisms authorize identities, while assurance layers certify proposed actions; neither alone provides a mandatory enforcement point for certified authority at the moment of mutation. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of ensuring certified authority in autonomous agent workflows, by building a Sovereign Execution Broker that enforces certificate-bound authority, resulting in a more secure runtime environment. The SEB acts as a runtime enforcement boundary for agentic infrastructure, consuming certificates to verify proposed actions. This research aims to provide a mandatory enforcement point for certified authority in cloud, deployment, and data-control workflows.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure with autonomous agents, here is what to do: review your access-control mechanisms, assess the use of assurance layers, and consider implementing a Sovereign Execution Broker to enforce certified authority at the point of mutation. case_studies.title: Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
case_studies.abstract: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluator bias in large language models by creating a framework to measure how biases spread across multiple agents. The researchers built Contagion Networks and tested it in a controlled experiment with three agents. The result shows that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents.

This research is focused on large language models and evaluator bias, which is more relevant to AI and machine learning applications. case_studies.title: The Significance of Style Diversity in Annotation-Free Synthetic Data Generation
case_studies.abstract: Generating high-utility synthetic data for intent classification typically requires human-annotated seed data, which is often unavailable in fast-paced industrial settings. In this paper, we propose a framework for synthetic dialogue generation that works entirely without human-annotated data, relying solely on intent definitions. Our proposed dialogue generation framework utilizes two different types of topic and style attributes to improve data diversity. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of generating high-quality synthetic data for intent classification without requiring human-annotated seed data. The authors built a framework that uses intent definitions and style diversity to generate synthetic dialogue. The result is a more diverse and realistic synthetic data set.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage machine learning models or natural language processing applications, check your current data generation methods to see if they rely on human-annotated data. This research may offer an alternative approach to generating synthetic data. It is not directly applicable to cloud infrastructure management, but may be relevant to teams working with AI and ML applications.

case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of forecasting Key Performance Measurements in 5G telecom networks by building a scalable framework called TelcoAgent, which enables accurate and explainable forecasting across diverse network cells. The result is a framework that can forecast multiple KPMs without needing site-specific training. This is relevant for telecom network management, particularly for those managing 5G infrastructure.

case_studies.title: TimeProVe: Propose, then Verify for Efficient Long Video Temporal Reasoning in Activities of Daily Living

TimeProVe combines lightweight modules and vision-language models to achieve this. It is not directly relevant to cloud infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages
case_studies.abstract: LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limited programming language support in LiveCodeBench, a benchmark for evaluating large language models. The team built Multi-LCB, which extends LiveCodeBench to support multiple programming languages. The result is a more comprehensive evaluation of large language models' code-generation capabilities.

case_studies.title: Calibration Without Comprehension: Diagnosing the Limits of Fine-Tuning LLMs for Vulnerability Detection in Systems Software
case_studies.abstract: Whether LLMs scoring well on vulnerability benchmarks genuinely reason about security or merely pattern-match on contaminated data remains unresolved. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of determining whether large language models (LLMs) can genuinely reason about security vulnerabilities or just pattern-match. The researchers built a framework called CWE-Trace to evaluate LLMs on vulnerability detection. The result shows the limitations of using LLMs for vulnerability detection in systems software.
